title: Flip graph connectivity in three dimensions
formal:
For every finite point set \(P\subset\mathbb R^3\) with \(|P|\ge4\) and no four points coplanar, is the graph of all geometric tetrahedralizations of \(P\) connected under \(2\leftrightarrow3\) bistellar flips?

A tetrahedralization must use exactly the vertices \(P\), consist of straight, nondegenerate tetrahedra meeting along common faces, and cover \(\operatorname{conv}(P)\). A legal flip replaces two tetrahedra filling a convex triangular bipyramid by the three tetrahedra with the same five vertices and the same union, or performs the reverse replacement. Every intermediate tetrahedralization must retain all points of \(P\) as vertices.

Equivalently, for every such \(P\) and every pair \(T,T'\) of its tetrahedralizations, must there exist a finite sequence \(T=T_0,T_1,\ldots,T_m=T'\) in which each consecutive pair differs by one legal flip?
why: This is a basic reachability question for three-dimensional meshes: can local bistellar moves explore every tetrahedralization without changing the underlying points? A resolution would identify a fundamental difference, or an essential commonality, between planar triangulation algorithms and their three-dimensional counterparts.
status_note: Source-open in TOPP Problem 28 (entry history through 22 December 2008) and explicitly retained as open in the introduction of Wagner–Welzl, Discrete & Computational Geometry 68 (2022). On 16 September 2026 the source’s fixed-vertex move restriction, the 2007 regular-triangulation consequence and the 2022 discussion were checked. Bounded subsequent searches found no proof or geometric counterexample for this precise target. The regular result was checked through its publisher abstract and the TOPP statement, not by independent verification of its full proof. This records dated explicit openness and limited later review, not an exhaustive current-status certification.

progress.text: TOPP attributes the question to work of Edelsbrunner, Preparata and West and of Joe on three-dimensional tetrahedralization and local transformations.
The source records disconnected higher-dimensional triangulation spaces and abstract nonrealizable three-dimensional counterexamples. These do not settle the geometric general-position target.
Pournin and Liebling establish the fixed-vertex connectivity result for regular triangulations, leaving arbitrary tetrahedralizations outside this theorem.
Wagner and Welzl retain three- and four-dimensional connectivity as open while resolving stronger planar connectivity questions.

importance.reason: A longstanding central problem in computational geometry and triangulation theory, with direct relevance to local mesh transformations and a sharp distinction between geometric and abstract complexes. The simple local moves conceal a global connectivity question that remains unsettled beyond regular triangulations.

sentences: A tetrahedralization divides the convex hull of a fixed three-dimensional point set into tetrahedra.
A local flip replaces two tetrahedra by three, or reverses that replacement, while retaining the same five vertices.
The question asks whether every pair of tetrahedralizations can be joined by such moves when no four input points are coplanar.
All intermediate meshes must keep every original point as a vertex at its original coordinates.
Regular tetrahedralizations are known to be connected, but the unrestricted geometric question remains open in the checked sources.

definitions:
The set \(P\) is finite and consists of distinct points with arbitrary real coordinates in ordinary three-dimensional Euclidean space. General position here means that every four distinct points are affinely independent, equivalently that no four lie in a common plane. Together with \(|P|\ge4\), this ensures a three-dimensional convex hull and nonzero volume for every tetrahedron with four vertices in \(P\). Points may lie in the interior of \(\operatorname{conv}(P)\); they are not assumed to be in convex position. No additional condition on cospherical points is imposed.

For a finite set of points \(A\), its convex hull \(\operatorname{conv}(A)\) is the set of all convex combinations of points of \(A\), with \(\operatorname{conv}(\varnothing)=\varnothing\). A geometric tetrahedron with vertex set \(A\subset P\), \(|A|=4\), is the closed set \(\operatorname{conv}(A)\). Its faces are the convex hulls of subsets of its vertices, including vertices, edges, triangles, the tetrahedron itself and the empty face.

A tetrahedralization is a collection \(T\) of four-element subsets of \(P\) satisfying all of the following conditions. Every point of \(P\) belongs to some member of \(T\). The union of the corresponding closed tetrahedra is \(\operatorname{conv}(P)\). For every \(A,B\in T\),
\[\operatorname{conv}(A)\cap\operatorname{conv}(B)=\operatorname{conv}(A\cap B).\]
Thus different tetrahedra have disjoint interiors and any intersection is their common face; overlaps, crossing faces and hanging vertices inside another tetrahedron are excluded. All faces of the tetrahedra are understood to belong to the resulting simplicial complex. This is a full geometric triangulation, not merely an abstract complex homeomorphic to a ball. No extra vertices, curved faces or gaps in the convex hull are allowed.

The local replacement can be specified by five distinct points \(a,b,c,d,e\in P\). They must all be vertices of their convex hull, and that hull must be the convex triangular bipyramid formed by the two tetrahedra \(\{a,b,c,d\}\) and \(\{a,b,c,e\}\) sharing triangle \(abc\). In particular, \(d\) and \(e\) are on opposite sides of the plane of \(a,b,c\). Write
\[U_2=\bigl\{\{a,b,c,d\},\{a,b,c,e\}\bigr\},\qquad U_3=\bigl\{\{a,b,d,e\},\{b,c,d,e\},\{c,a,d,e\}\bigr\}.\]
These are the two tetrahedralizations of this bipyramid: \(U_2\) uses the interior triangle \(abc\), while \(U_3\) uses the interior edge \(de\). A \(2\)-to-\(3\) flip is allowed when \(U_2\subseteq T\) and
\[T'=(T\setminus U_2)\cup U_3\]
is a tetrahedralization of the same \(P\), with the replaced tetrahedra and the new tetrahedra having exactly the same geometric union. A \(3\)-to-\(2\) flip is the inverse operation under the same conditions. Requiring both configurations to be valid tetrahedralizations makes the local move compatible with all tetrahedra outside the replaced region.

The flip graph \(\mathcal F(P)\) is the finite undirected graph whose vertices are these tetrahedralizations and whose edges join pairs related by one such flip. Reversing a legal move is legal. Connectivity means that every pair of graph vertices can be joined by a finite path. The path may have length zero when the two tetrahedralizations coincide. No polynomial bound, sharp diameter, monotonicity condition or prescribed target triangulation is part of the proposition.

Only \(2\)-to-\(3\) and \(3\)-to-\(2\) moves are permitted. A \(1\)-to-\(4\) move inserts an interior vertex into a tetrahedron, and a \(4\)-to-\(1\) move removes a vertex; neither is allowed, even if the point is restored later. Points cannot be moved or perturbed along a path. Allowing such operations changes the graph under study.

The quantifier order is \(\forall P\;\forall T,T'\;\exists m\ge0\;\exists(T_i)_{i=0}^m\). All tetrahedralizations and all intermediate coordinates refer to the same fixed geometric point set. A negative answer consists of a set meeting the general-position hypothesis and two valid tetrahedralizations in different components, with a proof that no finite legal path joins them. Merely showing that one particular greedy rule gets stuck, or displaying an abstract nonrealizable tetrahedral complex, is insufficient.

Regular tetrahedralizations are a special class mentioned in the known results. A tetrahedralization \(T\) is regular if there is a height assignment \(w:P\to\mathbb R\) such that, for each \(A\in T\), an affine function \(\ell_A:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R\) equals \(w\) on the four points of \(A\) and is strictly below \(w\) at every point of \(P\setminus A\). These are the tetrahedralizations obtained by projecting the simplicial lower hull of the lifted points. The target includes nonregular tetrahedralizations as well. It is an exact geometric existence question; there is no coordinate encoding, running-time or approximation tolerance to optimize.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of connectivity for every finite point set in the stated general position. A positive proof must establish a finite legal \(2\leftrightarrow3\) path between every pair of full geometric tetrahedralizations, with all intermediate complexes using the same point coordinates and vertex set. No efficient path-finding algorithm or polynomial path length is required. A negative proof must establish the general position and geometric validity of a counterexample and prove that two tetrahedralizations lie in different components of its full flip graph. A result only for regular triangulations, higher-dimensional point sets, abstract complexes, or paths that remove or add vertices does not settle the target. Numerical experiments and approximate coordinate pictures alone are insufficient.

source_formulation.text: TOPP Problem 28 asks whether tetrahedralizations of a general-position point set in three-dimensional space form a connected graph when adjacency is restricted to replacing two tetrahedra by three, or three by two. The source specifies general position as having no four coplanar points and distinguishes results that permit vertex insertion or deletion.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of TOPP Problem 28; the fixed geometric vertex set and the allowed two-to-three moves are retained

context_blocks.text: A tetrahedral mesh can be changed locally while leaving its boundary and vertex coordinates fixed. Connectivity asks whether these basic local changes can in principle reach every mesh of the same point set, or whether the space of meshes splits into inaccessible regions.

For planar point sets, diagonal flips connect all triangulations. This is an important structural basis for local triangulation algorithms. The analogous conclusion in three dimensions does not follow just from the existence of tetrahedralizations or from the planar argument.

For regular triangulations with a fixed vertex set, Pournin and Liebling prove connectivity by paths that preserve faces common to the two endpoints. TOPP explicitly notes that in the three-dimensional general-position setting this uses the required two-to-three and three-to-two moves. The unrestricted question is whether nonregular tetrahedralizations can also be connected within the full graph.

There are disconnected triangulation spaces in higher dimensions, and TOPP records nonrealizable abstract tetrahedral complexes with no allowed flips. These show why dimensional and geometric-realizability hypotheses matter, but neither gives a counterexample for the three-dimensional point sets in this question.

Wagner and Welzl’s 2022 paper proves stronger connectivity results in the plane and explicitly says in its introduction that connectivity remains open in dimensions three and four. It also carefully distinguishes full triangulations, which retain all points, from partial triangulations that may omit interior points.

A positive answer would establish reachability by the permitted local moves, rather than a running-time guarantee for a mesh optimization heuristic. Even a connected graph can have long routes, and connectivity does not ensure that an objective improves on every move.
